description:
Yellow poplar also known as Tulip Tree, (Liriodendron tulipifera) are found in valleys and stream bottoms at elevations bellow 300 meters of the northern end range. However, in the southern Appalachian’s it can grow on a variety of sites including stream bottoms, coves, & moist slopes. Elevation for that is about 1370 meters. 

During the growth period, the first year ranges from a few centimeters to more than 1ft on better site areas. With lots of light, it starts to rapidly grow and within 5 years the tree can be anywhere from 10-18ft tall. 

April is the start of the flowering season in the southern US, in the northern US flowers bloom in June. Flowers are pale green or yellow, with orange band on tepals. 

Considered one of the largest trees in North America, height of 192 ft. Diameter of trunks depend on the height of tree but on larger trees the diameter is 4-6ft. But, can grow more in width. Pyramidal crown. Bark is brown, furrowed, smells aromatic and bitter. Branches are smooth sometimes reddish growing into dark grey then brown. Wood color is light yellow to brown, sapwood is creamy white. Fruit: narrow light brown cone, dispersed by wind.

The leaf I looked at was a little bit smaller than my hand, so I'd say it was about four inches wide and maybe four and a half or five inches tall. The trunk of the tree had what I would call medium depth furrows to it's decently chunky bark. The bark wasn't peeling at all like some other trees do. For weather, it was partly cloudy in the morning and it got sunnier as the day moved along. The temperature at the time of the photo was 72 degrees fahrenheit, and the high and low for the day were 72 and 53 degrees fahrenheit respectively. Wind was traveling 3 mph SW. Humidity was sitting at 64%. There was 0.1" of rainfall in the 24 hours before the time of the photo as well. In terms of other species seen, there were many pin oak trees around the tulip tree. No birds or bees or any other organisms were really seen, but I would not have been shocked to see pollinators around any of the flowers present on the tree. That's all I have for this week's species account.

Disturbed lowland woods with a canopy of various native hardwoods, a serious invasion of Norway maple, and a typical understory composed of mostly invasive species like Privets, Burning Bush, and Multiflora Rose.

The southwest side of the loop has almost no native tree regeneration. There are some huge bitternut and shagbark hickories here, but almost every young tree growing here is a Norway maple. There are probably a couple hundred of them between 2-6" that would be great to remove at this stage. The northern section of the loop is dense with Ligustrum obtusifolium. Besides Carpinus carolinana and a few Viburnum prunifolium, a native understory is non-existent.

description:
This is the famous **Davie Poplar**, approximately 350 years of age.

At dusk, hundreds and hundreds of Chimney Swifts swirl in vortex above, before darting into the hollow trunk to spend the night. An Eastern Gray Squirrel, however, awaits their arrival, fulfilling its classification as an omnivore. [see 3rd photo].

30 years ago, Dr. Jerome Jackson had amongst the slide set for his students of Ornithology, a photo that elicited primal gasps of horror and shock. The photo showed in gruesome detail an Eastern Gray Squirrel holding a male Northern Cardinal like an ice cream cone. The head of the cardinal had been devoured.

The memory of that photo sprang to mind when I espied the Eastern Gray Squirrel lingering around the hollow into which the Chimney Swifts would descend. And then it quietly slipped in to greet them upon their arrival.

Winter tree ID 
1- bark

4- leaf scars detail
5- seed cone
6- individual seeds
7- leaf
8- pith diaphragmed; it helps to allow the cut twigs to dry for several hours or overnight for the dividing partitions to become evident

Another characteristic for ID is the aromatic odor of the cut twigs.

Scale is in inches 
* NOTE - the dark spots on the twigs and buds in photos 2-5 are scale insects
These are pretty common around here, especially in and near young forests like this one.
